item.stem: A solid alloy contains metals X and Y. Their atomic radii are X: 128 pm and Y: 135 pm. The alloy conducts electricity. Which particulate-level model best explains both the alloy’s structure and its electrical conductivity?

choices.choice_text: Y atoms occupy gaps between X atoms, and mobile, delocalized valence electrons carry current throughout the solid.
choices.rationale: This is the interstitial-versus-substitutional trap: it places similarly sized atoms in lattice gaps. Interstitial alloys instead involve atoms significantly smaller than the host atoms; the conductivity explanation is sound. Fix: Compare atomic radii before deciding whether added atoms fill gaps or replace host atoms.

choices.choice_text: Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and positive metal ions move through the solid to carry current.
choices.rationale: This is the mobile-ion trap: it assigns electrical conduction in a solid metal to moving positive ions. The substitutional structure fits the radii, but current is carried by mobile, delocalized electrons, not ions traveling through the lattice. Fix: Identify which charged particles can move throughout a solid metal.

choices.choice_text: Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and valence electrons confined to individual metal atoms carry current throughout the solid.
choices.rationale: This is the localized-electron trap: it treats metallic valence electrons as belonging to individual atoms. Electrons confined to individual atoms cannot account for conduction throughout the solid; metallic valence electrons are delocalized and mobile. Fix: Check whether the model lets valence electrons move throughout the entire solid.

choices.choice_text: Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and mobile, delocalized valence electrons carry current throughout the solid.
choices.rationale: The comparable atomic radii favor a substitutional alloy, in which Y atoms occupy some host lattice positions. Valence electrons are delocalized and mobile throughout the solid, allowing them to carry electrical current.

item.stem: A steel wire carries current in an electrical circuit. The steel consists mainly of iron with a small amount of carbon added. For this model, the atomic radii are 126 pm for iron and 77 pm for carbon. Which description connects the wire’s alloy structure with its ability to conduct electricity?

choices.choice_text: Carbon atoms substitute for iron atoms at lattice sites; delocalized valence electrons move through the wire and transport charge.
choices.rationale: The interstitial-versus-substitutional trap assigns the smaller carbon atoms to replacement sites. Their substantially smaller radius supports occupancy of gaps instead, although the electron-based explanation of conductivity is sound. Fix: Compare the added atoms’ size with the host atoms’ size before assigning their positions.

choices.choice_text: Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; positive iron ions travel through the wire and transport charge.
choices.rationale: The mobile-ion trap mistakes the metal ions for the moving charge carriers. The interstitial structure fits the radii, but solid-metal conduction involves mobile electrons, not ions traveling through the framework. Fix: Identify the mobile charge carriers in the solid before explaining its conductivity.

choices.choice_text: Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; delocalized valence electrons move through the wire and transport charge.
choices.rationale: Carbon atoms are substantially smaller than iron atoms, supporting an interstitial structure with carbon in the gaps. The mobile valence electrons belong to the metallic solid as a whole, so they can transport charge through the wire.

choices.choice_text: Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; valence electrons remain attached to individual iron atoms while transporting charge through the wire.
choices.rationale: The localized-electron trap confines valence electrons to separate atoms. Although the alloy structure fits the radii, electrons restricted to individual atoms cannot explain charge transport throughout the wire. Fix: Check whether the proposed electrons can travel beyond individual atoms throughout the wire.

object.defect: Well posed. Carbon (77 pm) is much smaller than iron (126 pm), so steel is an interstitial alloy, which rules out A. Metals conduct through delocalized valence electrons, not through moving ions or electrons bound to single atoms, which rules out B and D. Only C satisfies both parts of the question.

item.stem: A sample of a pure metal is hammered into a thinner sheet without breaking. Which particulate-level model best explains this observation?

choices.choice_text: Layers of positive metal ions slide past one another while the mobile, delocalized valence electrons continue to hold the solid together.
choices.rationale: Metallic bonding is not restricted to individual pairs of atoms. The delocalized electrons maintain attractions to the positive metal ions as the layers shift, allowing the metal to change shape without breaking.

choices.choice_text: Layers of alternating positive and negative ions slide past one another while attractions between oppositely charged ions hold the solid together.
choices.rationale: Ionic-lattice confusion: a pure metal contains positive metal ions surrounded by delocalized electrons, not alternating positive and negative ions. This model gives the metal the wrong charged components. Fix: Identify the positive ions and delocalized electrons before describing how a metal deforms.

choices.choice_text: The positive metal ions remain in their original positions while the surrounding electron sea becomes thinner and wider.
choices.rationale: Electron-only deformation error: changing the electron distribution alone cannot explain the sample’s new shape while all metal ions remain fixed. The arrangement of metal ions must also change during deformation. Fix: Check whether the model allows the metal ions to move into the new shape.

choices.choice_text: Layers of metal atoms slide past one another because each atom’s valence electrons remain localized on that atom.
choices.rationale: Localized-electron misconception: metallic valence electrons belong to the solid as a whole, rather than remaining on individual atoms. Localized electrons do not represent the shared electron sea that maintains cohesion as layers shift. Fix: Check whether the model distributes valence electrons throughout the solid rather than on individual atoms.

object.defect: Malleability is explained by the electron-sea model. Layers of metal cations shift past one another, and the delocalized electrons keep the bonding nondirectional, so the sheet does not fracture (A). B describes an ionic solid, where shifting layers would bring like charges together and cause shattering, so it is wrong. C is wrong because the cations must move for the sheet to change shape. D is wrong because metallic valence electrons are delocalized, not localized on each atom.

item.stem: A straight wire made of pure copper is bent into a loop without cracking. Which particulate-level description best accounts for the wire’s ability to change shape while remaining intact?

choices.choice_text: Positive and negative copper ions shift relative to one another, while attractions between these oppositely charged ions keep the wire intact.
choices.rationale: Ionic-lattice confusion: this description incorrectly assigns both positive and negative ions to metallic copper. Its charged components are positive metal ions and delocalized electrons, not oppositely charged ions. Fix: Identify the charged components of a metal before explaining their attractions.

choices.choice_text: Positive copper ions stay at their original locations, while only the surrounding electron sea curves into the wire’s new shape.
choices.rationale: Electron-only deformation error: reshaping the electron sea while keeping every copper ion fixed cannot account for the wire becoming a loop. The metal ions must rearrange as the wire bends. Fix: Check that the proposed model moves the ions when the wire changes shape.

choices.choice_text: Copper atoms shift relative to one another, while valence electrons confined to their individual atoms keep the wire intact.
choices.rationale: Localized-electron misconception: confining valence electrons to individual copper atoms misrepresents metallic bonding. The electrons are mobile throughout the solid and provide attractions that maintain cohesion as the ions rearrange. Fix: Verify that the model allows valence electrons to move throughout the metal.

choices.choice_text: Positive copper ions shift relative to one another, while mobile valence electrons distributed throughout the solid maintain attractions that hold it together.
choices.rationale: The mobile, delocalized electrons attract positive copper ions even as the ions rearrange. These attractions preserve cohesion during bending because metallic bonding does not depend on fixed bonds between particular pairs of atoms.

item.stem: A copper-rich brass strip serves as an electrical connector. Copper and zinc have approximate atomic radii of 128 pm and 134 pm, respectively. The strip carries electric current while remaining solid. Which particulate model explains both the zinc atoms’ locations and the strip’s electrical conductivity?

choices.choice_text: Zinc atoms fit into spaces between copper atoms in the metallic array; delocalized valence electrons move through the solid to transport charge.
choices.rationale: Interstitial-alloy trap: This model places similarly sized atoms into gaps that accommodate much smaller atoms. Zinc’s radius is close to copper’s, supporting replacement rather than gap filling. Fix: Compare the added atoms’ radii with the host atoms’ radii before assigning their locations.

choices.choice_text: Zinc atoms take the places of some copper atoms in the metallic array; positive metal ions travel through the solid to transport charge.
choices.rationale: Ion-migration trap: This explanation mistakes positive metal ions for the mobile charge carriers. During electrical conduction, the ions remain in the solid’s array while delocalized electrons transport charge. Fix: Identify the mobile charge carriers in the solid before explaining its conductivity.

choices.choice_text: Zinc atoms take the places of some copper atoms in the metallic array; valence electrons restricted to their individual atoms transport charge through the solid.
choices.rationale: Localized-electron trap: Restricting valence electrons to individual atoms prevents them from transporting charge across the strip. The metallic model instead allows delocalized electrons to move throughout the solid. Fix: Test whether the proposed electrons can travel across the entire connector.

choices.choice_text: Zinc atoms take the places of some copper atoms in the metallic array; delocalized valence electrons move through the solid to transport charge.
choices.rationale: The similar atomic radii support a substitutional structure, with zinc occupying sites otherwise occupied by copper. The mobility of delocalized valence electrons throughout the metallic solid explains its electrical conductivity.
